questions.subject: ENGLISH_LANGUAGE
questions.learningObjective: Analyze whether a clinical argument assumes an unstated generalisation

stimulus.body: A note argues 'This drug worked in our clinic, so it will work nationally.'

questions.stem: Is an assumed warrant present?

options.text: No, because it worked in the clinic.
Yes, because drugs never work nationally.
Yes, because it assumes clinic results transfer nationally.

questions.explanation: The argument assumes clinic results transfer nationally. Representativeness is assumed, not shown.
questions.hint: Does the clinic represent the nation?

questions.learningObjective: Identify the hidden premise in a clinical prevention argument
questions.stem: A note argues 'Prevention is cheaper, so we should fund prevention'; what hidden premise is assumed?

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LANGUAGE
questions.learningObjective: Evaluate whether a counterargument addresses the claim's evidence

stimulus.body: A note claims a therapy works based on 10 trials. A reviewer replies that 8 of the 10 trials were industry-funded.

questions.stem: Does the counterargument engage the claim?

options.text: Yes, because industry is always biased.

questions.explanation: Funding source may bias results, so the counterargument engages the evidence. Blanket bias and rejection miss the point.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LANGUAGE
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a clinician's note should not overstate limited findings
questions.stem: A note turns 'may help' into 'cures' in its conclusion; explain the risk.

answer.exemplar: Overstating tentative findings as cures misleads readers and clinicians, risking harmful decisions and eroding trust when results fail to replicate.

questions.explanation: Overstating evidence misleads and risks harm. Trust erodes if results fail to replicate.
questions.hint: What happens if the cure claim is wrong?

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LANGUAGE
questions.learningObjective: Analyze whether a note's rebuttal is proportional to the objection

stimulus.body: A note concedes a drug has a 0.1 percent rash risk, then writes three pages defending against it.

questions.stem: Is the rebuttal proportional?

options.text: Yes, because any risk needs full defence.
No, because the response exceeds the risk magnitude.
No, because rebuttals are never useful.

questions.explanation: A 0.1 percent risk does not warrant three pages. The response is disproportionate to the magnitude.
questions.hint: Compare response length to risk size.
